newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Motivations differ as Europeans eye Mideast role.
newsitem.headline: Motivations differ as Europeans eye Mideast role.

text.p: The latest crisis in the Middle East has provided European countries with an opportunity to grab a long sought-after diplomatic role in peace negotiations dominated by Washington.
France, Russia and the European Union have all launched initiatives to bring themselves closer to the peace process that has stalled since the election of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Arab leaders have also leapt at the chance of having players other than Washington brought into the picture.

Egypt's foreign minister, Amr Moussa, urged his EU counterparts on Monday to bring their influences to bear on Israel to stick with its peace process commitments; Palestinian President Yasser Arafat is giving a similar message on a mini-tour of European capitals.

All agree that there is a danger to Europe from renewed violence in the Middle East, but the motivations of the European countries to become involved are mixed. Some see a chance to exercise diplomatic leadership as the United States struggles, while others are just keen to see their interests served.

"They (the Europeans) are obviously concerned about what happens, but there is a bit of Schadenfreude, of being happy that your brother is hurting," said Shireen Hunter, Middle East specialist at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS).

Within the 15-nation European Union, France has made most of the running, culminating in a highly publicised trip to the region by French President Jacques Chirac that included a sharp exchange with Israeli security forces.

Chirac's foray is seen in EU circles as motivated both by France's traditional, Gaullist desire to be heard on the world stage -- sometimes as an alternative to the United States -- and by its long-standing role in the Middle East.
For most other EU countries, however, the motivation is less to take a lead as to ensure that as the major financial donor to the peace process, the EU has its place at the diplomatic table.
The contrast was apparent on Monday at an EU foreign minister's meeting in Luxembourg.

France's Herve de Charette was cock-a-hoop over the EU's appointment of a special envoy to the Middle East peace process, seeing it as "good news for Europe, good news for the Middle East and, I hope, good news for peace."
Others, were more sanguine. German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel warned the EU not to overstretch itself and to coordinate closely with Washington.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, who has recently represented the EU in the region, emphasised that the United States -- where there is a presidential election next week -- must not believe Europe is trying to muscle in.
"We are all very conscious that Europe is the major donor to the region and the major trading partner," he said. "We can assist the United States."

Miguel Angel Moratinos, Spain's ambassador to Israel and the new EU envoy, echoed this in an interview with Radio France International, adding he intended to act as a go-between to calm tensions rather than demand a place at the negotiating table.
"I believe that the role of the Union is not so much to sit at a table as to transmit political messages and show one's economic and financial availability," he said.
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters the envoy would "reinforce the action of the peace partners including that of the American coordinator Dennis Ross".
Moscow has also launched an initiative to get involved in the peace process with the arrival in Damascus on Monday of Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, a long-time Arabist.

Russian foreign policy analysts say U.S.-French rivalry in the region, the worry among Arab leaders that Washington is too pro-Israel, and the general faltering of the process meant the time was right time for Russia to return to the scene.
"The Russian Foreign Ministry has received signals from states in the region that new initiatives by Primakov will be most welcome," the television current affairs programme Itogi said on Sunday.
But CEPS's Hunter said with success for Europe far from guaranteed, it was not clear what Russia could offer.
"Europe brings more than Russia. You have to have money, you have to have arms and you have to have something to give as an incentive or a punishment," she said. "Russia doesn't have any of that."
